############################# # Exercise Group Introduction #############################
BEGIN_PGML Does the table show that [`x`] and [`y`] have a linear relationship?
END_PGML
###### # Body ######
BEGIN_PGML >> [@DataTable( [ [ [PGML('[`x`]'), rowbottom => '2', midrule => '1',], PGML('[`y`]'), ], [ PGML('[`[$x[0]]`]'), PGML('[`[$y[0]]`]'), ], [ PGML('[`[$x[1]]`]'), PGML('[`[$y[1]]`]'), ], [ PGML('[`[$x[2]]`]'), PGML('[`[$y[2]]`]'), ], [ PGML('[`[$x[3]]`]'), PGML('[`[$y[3]]`]'), ], [ PGML('[`[$x[4]]`]'), PGML('[`[$y[4]]`]'), ], [ PGML('[`[$x[5]]`]'), PGML('[`[$y[5]]`]'), ], ], align => '*{2}{r}', valign => 'middle',);@]* <<
[_]{$yes}{5}
END_PGML
########## # Solution ##########
BEGIN_PGML_SOLUTION The [`x`]-values in this table jump erratically. However, if we compute the rate of change between consecutive rows in the table, the result is always [$m]. For example, the rate of change between the first and second rows is
[``` \frac{[$y[1]]-[$y[0]]}{[$x[1]]-[$x[0]]}=\frac{[$ydiff]}{[$xdiff]}=[$m] \text{.}```]
END_PGML_SOLUTION
